question_text: A 63-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of progressive blurring and darkening of her vision in the right eye. Upon waking up in the morning, she suddenly started seeing multiple dark streaks. She has migraines and type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed at her last health maintenance examination 20 years ago. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years. Her only medication is sumatriptan. Her vitals are within normal limits. Ophthalmologic examination shows visual acuity of 20/40 in the left eye and 20/100 in the right eye. The fundus is obscured and difficult to visualize on fundoscopic examination of the right eye. The red reflex is diminished on the right. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

                    ### Question
                    A 63-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of progressive blurring and darkening of her vision in the right eye. Upon waking up in the morning, she suddenly started seeing multiple dark streaks. She has migraines and type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed at her last health maintenance examination 20 years ago. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years. Her only medication is sumatriptan. Her vitals are within normal limits. Ophthalmologic examination shows visual acuity of 20/40 in the left eye and 20/100 in the right eye. The fundus is obscured and difficult to visualize on fundoscopic examination of the right eye. The red reflex is diminished on the right. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Central retinal vein occlusion
opb. Central retinal artery occlusion
opc. Cataract
opd. Migraine aura
ope. Vitreous hemorrhage

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The 63-year-old woman presents with sudden vision changes, specifically progressive blurring and darkening of vision in the right eye, along with multiple dark streaks. The fundoscopic examination reveals an obscured fundus and diminished red reflex in the right eye. These findings are consistent with vitreous hemorrhage, which can occur due to her risk factors of diabetes and smoking. While central retinal vein occlusion is also a possibility given her vascular risk factors, the acute nature of her symptoms and the specific findings of obscured fundus and diminished red reflex strongly suggest vitreous hemorrhage as the most likely diagnosis. Other options like cataract and migraine aura are less likely due to the sudden onset and significant visual acuity changes. Therefore, the most likely diagnosis is vitreous hemorrhage.
